Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim:
The product law $\mu\otimes
u$ is a Borel probability on $\mathbb R^d	imes\mathbb R^d$ with marginals $\mu,
u$ by [F1], so it belongs to $\Gamma(\mu,
u)$. Thus the coupling set in the definition is nonempty.

By the inequality in [F2] and the finite second moments of $\mu,
u$, Tonelli gives $\int|x-y|^2d(\mu\otimes
u)\le2\int|x|^2d\mu+2\int|y|^2d
u<\infty.$ All coupling costs are nonnegative, so their infimum is finite and nonnegative; its square root in the displayed definition is therefore a finite real number.

citations.quote: Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]]. A compatible complete metric may be fixed for a construction; it is not additional data in the law. The empty space admits no such law, since its measure must be both zero and one.

For Borel probabilities $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, the following are equivalent: (i) $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$; (ii) integrals converge for all bounded uniformly continuous real tests; (iii) $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F; (iv) $\liminf_n\mu_n(G)\ge\mu(G)$ for every open G; (v) $\mu_n(A)\to\mu(A)$ for every Borel A with $\mu(\partial A)=0$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $X,Y$ be second-countable topological spaces and give $X\times Y$ the
product topology. Then
$$\mathcal B(X\times Y)=\mathcal B(X)\otimes\mathcal B(Y).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. If
$E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, then $E_x \in \mathcal B$ for every
$x \in X$ and $E^y \in \mathcal A$ for every $y \in Y$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: Let $G\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $t_n\to t$. Narrow continuity gives $\mu_{t_n}\Rightarrow\mu_t$, so [F2] gives $\mu_t(G)\le\liminf_n\mu_{t_n}(G)$. Thus $t\mapsto\mu_t(G)$ is lower semicontinuous and hence Borel measurable.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the Borel sets $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for which $t\mapsto\mu_t(A)$ is measurable. It contains the whole space because each section is a probability. If $A\in\mathcal D$, then $\mu_t(A^c)=1-\mu_t(A)$, so $A^c\in\mathcal D$. For pairwise disjoint $A_j\in\mathcal D$, countable additivity gives $\mu_t(\bigcup_jA_j)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j=0}^N\mu_t(A_j)$, a measurable increasing limit. Hence $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system. The open sets form a pi-system generating the Borel sigma-algebra and belong to $\mathcal D$ by step 1.1, so [F3] and [F9] give $\mathcal D=\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$. Together with [F4], this proves that $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is a probability kernel.

By [F5], a product-Borel set $E$ is measurable for $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$. Its sections $E_t$ are Borel by [F6]. Since $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is a probability kernel by step 1.2, [F7] applied to $\mathbf1_E$ shows that $t\mapsto\mu_t(E_t)$ is measurable. Thus $M(E)=\int_0^T\mu_t(E_t)dt$ is defined; $M(\varnothing)=0$ and $M([0,T]\times\mathbb R^d)=\int_0^T1dt=T$.

If $E_j$ are disjoint product-Borel sets, their sections are disjoint and $\mu_t((\bigcup_jE_j)_t)=\sum_j\mu_t((E_j)_t)$. Integrating the increasing partial sums and using [F8] gives $M(\bigcup_jE_j)=\sum_jM(E_j)$; with step 1.2 this makes $M$ a finite Borel measure. For an indicator, the iterated-integral formula is the definition of $M$; finite nonnegative simple combinations give it for simple functions. For arbitrary nonnegative product-Borel $f$, use [F9] to choose $s_n\uparrow f$ and apply [F8] to both $M$ and the time-section integrals. This proves $\int f\,dM=\int_0^T\int f(t,x)d\mu_t(x)dt$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to $\alpha$ with its second coordinate y as conditioning variable, obtaining a probability kernel $K_y(dx)$ with $\alpha(A\times B)=\int_BK_y(A)d\rho(y)$. The supplier conditions on the second marginal, so for $\beta$ first define the coordinate swap $S(y,z)=(z,y)$ and $\widehat\beta=S_\#\beta$ on $\mathbb R^{d_3}\times\mathbb R^{d_2}$. By [F7], this is a Borel probability whose second marginal is the common law $\rho$. Apply [F2] to $\widehat\beta$ to obtain a probability kernel $L_y(dz)$ with $\widehat\beta(C\times B)=\int_BL_y(C)d\rho(y)$, equivalently $\beta(B\times C)=\int_BL_y(C)d\rho(y)$. Thus for every Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_1}$, $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_2}$, and $C\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_3}$ both joint laws are disintegrated over the same conditioning law.

For each $y$, let $Q_y=K_y\otimes L_y$, the product probability on $\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\mathbb R^{d_3}$. For a rectangle $A\times C$, $Q_y(A\times C)=K_y(A)L_y(C)$ is measurable in $y$. The sets $D$ for which $y\mapsto Q_y(D)$ is measurable form a lambda-system: the whole space has value one, complements have value $1-Q_y(D)$, and disjoint unions have value the increasing limit of finite sums. Rectangles form a pi-system generating the product Borel sigma-algebra by [F1] and [F4]. Thus [F4] proves measurability for every Borel $D$. The same lambda-system argument applied to rectangles $B\times A\times C$ in the variables $(y,x,z)$ shows that $y\mapsto Q_y(E_y)$ is measurable for each Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_2}\times\mathbb R^{d_1}\times\mathbb R^{d_3}$, where $E_y=\{(x,z):(y,x,z)\in E\}$.

Define $\widetilde\gamma(E)=\int Q_y(E_y)\,d\rho(y)$ on the product Borel sigma-algebra in the coordinate order $(y,x,z)$. It is nonnegative and has total mass one. For disjoint $E_j$, their sections are disjoint, so countable additivity of $Q_y$ followed by monotone convergence [F6] gives $\widetilde\gamma(\bigcup_jE_j)=\sum_j\widetilde\gamma(E_j)$. Hence $\widetilde\gamma$ is a Borel probability.

For Borel rectangles $B\times A\times\mathbb R^{d_3}$ and $B\times\mathbb R^{d_1}\times C$, the definition and the two identities in step 1.1 give respectively $\widetilde\gamma(B\times A\times\mathbb R^{d_3})=\int_BK_y(A)L_y(\mathbb R^{d_3})\,d\rho(y)=\alpha(A\times B)$ and $\widetilde\gamma(B\times\mathbb R^{d_1}\times C)=\int_BL_y(C)K_y(\mathbb R^{d_1})\,d\rho(y)=\beta(B\times C)$. Rectangles determine finite Borel measures by [F4], so these identities identify the two pair marginals in coordinate order $(y,x,z)$. Define the Borel coordinate permutation $P(y,x,z)=(x,y,z)$ and set $\gamma=P_\#\widetilde\gamma$, meaning $\gamma(H)=\widetilde\gamma(P^{-1}(H))$ for each Borel $H$; by [F7] this is a Borel probability. The coordinate projections satisfy $\operatorname{pr}_{x,y}\circ P(y,x,z)=(x,y)$ and $\operatorname{pr}_{y,z}\circ P(y,x,z)=(y,z)$, hence their pushforwards are exactly $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.
Assume AC. If $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ on a Polish space, then $\{\mu,\mu_1,\mu_2,\ldots\}$ is tight.

A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a metric space S is **tight** if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a compact $K\subseteq S$ such that $\mu(S\setminus K)<\varepsilon$ for every $\mu\in\mathcal A$. One K must work for the whole family. Compactness is [[def-metric-compactness]]. The empty family is tight, witnessed by the empty compact set.
Assume AC. A family $\mathcal A$ of Borel probabilities on a Polish space S is tight if and only if it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.
Bounded continuous real tests determine Borel probability measures on any metric space. In particular, weak limits are unique.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is [[def-metric-continuity]]. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. No completeness or coupling is required.
Bounded continuous real tests determine Borel probability measures on any metric space. In particular, weak limits are unique.

Let S be Polish in the sense of [[def-polish-space]]. A **Borel probability law on S** is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(S)$ with total mass one. Here $\mathcal B(S)$ is [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]] and probability measure means [[def-probability-measure]].    $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$

A D-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in each coordinate, so coordinate completeness gives a limit in S; bounding the first finitely many coordinate terms and then the geometric tail proves convergence in D. Sequences of rational vectors which are zero after finitely many coordinates form a countable dense subset, since the tail is arbitrarily small and each of finitely many coordinates can be approximated by rationals. derivations.claim: Suppose $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$. For each $n$ choose an optimal coupling $\pi_n$ and regard its coordinates as $X_n,Y$ with laws $\mu_n,\mu$. The cost gives $\int|X_n-Y|^2d\pi_n\to0$. For bounded continuous $\varphi$, choose a ball $B(0,K)$ with $\mu(B(0,K)^c)$ small. On the event $|Y|\le K$ and $|X_n-Y|\le\delta<1$, both points lie in the compact ball $\overline B(0,K+1)$, where $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous. The complement has probability at most $\mu(B(0,K)^c)+\delta^{-2}\int|X_n-Y|^2d\pi_n$. First choose $K$, then $δ$, and then $n$; the boundedness of $\varphi$ shows $\int\varphi d\mu_n-\int\varphi d\mu\to0$. Thus $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$.

Conversely suppose narrow convergence and the stated uniform tail condition. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so that the second-moment tails outside $Q=[-R,R]^d$ of all $\mu_n$ and of $\mu$ are less than $\varepsilon$; the tail of $\mu$ vanishes because $\mu\in\mathcal P_2$. Enlarge R slightly if necessary so its coordinate faces have zero $\mu$-mass. Partition each coordinate interval $[-R,R]$ by finitely many levels that are not atoms of the corresponding one-dimensional marginal of $\mu$, with mesh small enough that each resulting rectangular cell has diameter at most $\varepsilon$. Such levels exist because each probability has at most countably many atoms. Together with $Q^c$, these cells form a finite Borel partition $(C_i)_{i=0}^N$ whose boundaries have $\mu$-measure zero. By [F2], $a_{n,i}:=\mu_n(C_i)\to a_i:=\mu(C_i)$ for each $i$.

Write $Z_n=X_n-Y$ and $a_n=\int|Z_n|^2d\pi_n\to0$. For $R>K$, on $\{|X_n|>R\}$ either $|Y|>K$ or $|Z_n|>R-K$. Since $|X_n|^2\le2|Y|^2+2|Z_n|^2$, for every $n$, $\int_{|X_n|>R}|X_n|^2d\pi_n\le 2\int_{|Y|>K}|Y|^2d\pi_n+2K^2\frac{a_n}{(R-K)^2}+2a_n.$ Given a target $\eta>0$, first choose K so the first term is below $\eta/4$; then choose N so $a_n<\eta/8$ for $n\ge N$; then choose R>K so the middle term is below $\eta/8$ for all $n\ge N$. The last term is below $\eta/4$. Finally enlarge R so the finitely many tails for $n<N$ are below $\eta$. This proves the required uniform tail limit.

For each bounded cell $C_i\subset Q$, match mass $r_{n,i}=\min(a_{n,i},a_i)$. If $r_{n,i}>0$, take $r_{n,i}$ times the product of the probability measures $\mu_n|_{C_i}/a_{n,i}$ and $\mu|_{C_i}/a_i$; if $r_{n,i}=0$, use the zero measure. Its residual second moments are bounded by the two tails outside $Q$ plus $dR^2\sum_{i=1}^N|a_{n,i}-a_i|$ on each side: inside a bounded cell, unmatched mass is exactly the positive part of the difference of its two cell masses. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$, the function $W_2$ defined on $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ is a metric: for all $\mu,
u,\lambda\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ it is finite and nonnegative, $W_2(\mu,
u)=0$ exactly when $\mu=
u$, $W_2(\mu,
u)=W_2(
u,\mu)$, and $W_2(\mu,\lambda)\le W_2(\mu,
u)+W_2(
u,\lambda)$.

derivations.claim: Let $D=\mathbb Q\cap[0,T]$ together with $0,T$. For each $q\in D$, set $f_q(t)=W_2(\mu_t,\mu_q)$. The reverse triangle inequality and the assumed control give $|f_q(t)-f_q(s)|\le\int_s^t g(r)dr$, so $f_q$ is absolutely continuous. By [F1], it has a derivative almost everywhere, and because $g\in L^1$ by Holder, at common differentiability points of $f_q$ and $G(t)=\int_0^t g(r)dr$, difference quotients give $|f_q'(t)|\le g(t)$. Since $D$ is countable, outside one null set all these derivatives exist and are bounded by $g$. Define $m(t)=\sup_{q\in D}|f_q'(t)|$ there and set $m=0$ on the null set. Difference quotients along $h=1/n$ give measurable versions of the scalar derivatives, so $m$ is measurable; also $0\le m\le g$ almost everywhere and hence $m\in L^2(0,T)$.

For any $s,t$, continuity of the curve and density of $D$ imply $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)=\sup_{q\in D}|f_q(t)-f_q(s)|.$ The inequality from right to left is the reverse triangle inequality. For the other direction take $q_j\in D$ with $q_j\to s$; then $f_{q_j}(s)\to0$ and $f_{q_j}(t)\to W_2(\mu_t,\mu_s)$. For each q, [F1] and step 1.1 give $|f_q(t)-f_q(s)|\le\int_s^t|f_q'(r)|dr\le\int_s^t m(r)dr$. Taking the supremum proves $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t m(r)dr$.

The function $H(t)=\int_0^t m(r)dr$ is absolutely continuous, and [F1] gives $H'(t)=m(t)$ almost everywhere. At a time t where $H$ is differentiable and every $f_q$ is differentiable, step 2.1 gives $\limsup_{h\to0}\frac{W_2(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)}{|h|}\le m(t),$ while $W_2(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)\ge|f_q(t+h)-f_q(t)|$ gives a lower limit at least $|f_q'(t)|$ for every q. Taking the supremum yields a lower limit at least $m(t)$. Thus the metric derivative exists and equals $m(t)$ almost everywhere. The interval bound and square integrability follow from step 2.1 and $m\le g$.

Let h be any other nonnegative $L^2$ upper control. Repeating the scalar difference-quotient bound of step 1.1 with h gives $|f_q'(t)|\le h(t)$ almost everywhere for each q. Countability of D lets these inequalities hold off a single null set, so $m(t)\le h(t)$ there. By step 3.1, $|\dot\mu_t|=m(t)$ almost everywhere, proving leastness.

citations.quote: Let $T>0$ and let $t\mapsto\mu_t$ be a narrowly continuous curve of Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$, where narrow continuity means convergence against every bounded continuous real test function. For a product-Borel set $E\subseteq[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, write $E_t=\{x:(t,x)\in E\}$ and define $M(E)=\int_0^T\mu_t(E_t)dt$. Then $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is a probability kernel, $M$ is a finite Borel measure of total mass $T$, and for every nonnegative product-Borel $f$, $\int f\,dM=\int_0^T\int f(t,x)d\mu_t(x)dt$.

Fix $T>0$ and an integer $d\ge1$. Let $t\mapsto\mu_t$ be a narrowly continuous curve in $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ (so $t\mapsto\int f\,d\mu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous $f$), let $M$ be its space-time measure $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$, and let $v:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel. Its squared action is $A(\mu,v)=\int|v(t,x)|^2dM(t,x)$. If $A(\mu,v)<\infty$, say that $v$ solves the continuity equation for $\mu$ when
$$\int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}(\partial_t\varphi(t,x)+\nabla_x\varphi(t,x)\cdot v(t,x))\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt=0$$
for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)$. This is the distributional meaning of $\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(v_t\mu_t)=0$; the continuous representative fixes the endpoint laws.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

citations.quote: Assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). If $\mu$ is a Radon measure on an LCH space $X$ and $1\le p<\infty$, then $C_c(X)$ is dense in $L^p(\mu)$.

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;

   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last

no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.

followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

By [F1], this derivative tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$. Its difference quotient at $0$ is $uP_k(u)e^{-u}$ with $u=1/t$, which also tends to $0$ by [F1]; from the left it is zero. Induction therefore gives every derivative at $0$ equal to $0$ and continuous there, so $\phi$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$.

Set $\Phi(t)=\phi(t+1)\phi(1-t)$. By [F2], $\Phi$ is smooth. It vanishes for $t\notin[-1,1]$ and is positive for $-1<t<1$, so its support is $[-1,1]$. Let $I=\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi(t)\,dt$. The extreme-value bound [F3] makes $\Phi$ bounded on $[-1,1]$, so $I<\infty$. Since $\Phi(0)=e^{-2}>0$, continuity gives $\delta\in(0,1)$ with $\Phi(t)\ge e^{-2}/2$ on $[-\delta,\delta]$; [F3] gives $I\ge\delta e^{-2}>0$. Hence $\psi=\Phi/I$ is smooth, supported on $[-1,1]$, positive on $(-1,1)$, and has integral one.

Define $\rho_d(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\prod_{j=1}^d\psi(x_j)$. Repeated coordinatewise chain and product rules give every partial derivative as $\prod_{j=1}^d\psi^{(\alpha_j)}(x_j)$ for its multi-index $\alpha$, so all partial derivatives are continuous. The function is nonnegative, vanishes outside $[-1,1]^d$, and is positive at every point of $(-1,1)^d$; therefore its support is exactly that closed cube.

By [F4] and Tonelli, $\int\rho_d\,dx=(\int\rho_{d-1}\,dx)(\int\psi\,dt)$; the second factor is $1$ by step 2.1. Induction on $d$ proves $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d\,dx=1$.

first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Fix an initial pair $(s,x_0)$ and a closed ball $K=\overline B(x_0,r)$. On a sufficiently short one-sided interval $J$ adjoining $s$, absolute continuity of the integrals of $m_K,L_K$ gives $\int_Jm_K\le r$ and $\int_JL_K<1$. On continuous curves taking values in $K$, define $\Phi(X)(t)=x_0+\int_s^t b(q,X(q))dq,$ with the oriented integral when J lies to the left of s. The integrand is measurable because $q\mapsto(q,X(q))$ is continuous and b is Borel; it is integrable because $|b(q,X(q))|\le m_K(q)$ almost everywhere. The map preserves the closed sup-norm ball of radius r about the constant curve $x_0$, and $\|\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)\|_\infty\le(\int_JL_K)\|X-Y\|_\infty$. By [F1] it has a unique fixed point. The integral FTC [F2] makes this curve absolutely continuous and a solution almost everywhere.

If two solutions have the same value at one time and remain in a compact K on a common compact interval, partition that interval into finitely many subintervals on which $\int L_K<1$. On each subinterval beginning at a time where the solutions agree, their integral equations bound their sup-norm difference by $(\int L_K)$ times itself, so the difference is zero. Induction over the partition proves uniqueness throughout the common interval. Their union therefore defines a unique maximal solution. If a maximal endpoint $\tau$ lies in $(0,T)$ and the path stays in a compact K as $t\to\tau$, then $|\dot X(t)|\le m_K(t)$ makes $X(t)$ Cauchy at $\tau$. Its limit is finite, and step 1.1 restarted at that limit extends the solution, contradicting maximality. Hence an interior maximal endpoint forces the path to leave every compact set.

Assume the spatial derivative hypothesis. On a short interval and compact ball as in step 1.1, solutions from nearby initial points remain in a common compact ball. The contraction estimate gives $\|X(\cdot;s,x_0+h)-X(\cdot;s,x_0)\|_\infty\le C|h|$. Write $\Delta_h(t)=X(t;s,x_0+h)-X(t;s,x_0)$. The state-variable fundamental theorem of calculus [F3] gives $\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_s^t A_h(q)\Delta_h(q)dq,\quad A_h(q)=\int_0^1D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0)+\theta\Delta_h(q))d\theta.$ Put $A(q)=D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0))$ at the almost-everywhere times where the spatial differential exists, with value zero on its exceptional time set. The matrix equation $V(t)=I_d+\int_s^tA(q)V(q)dq$ has a unique continuous solution by the contraction argument of step 1.1, since $\int_JL_K<1$. Subtracting its product with h from the equation for $\Delta_h$ gives $\Delta_h(t)-V(t)h=\int_s^t A_h(q)(\Delta_h(q)-V(q)h)dq+\int_s^t(A_h(q)-A(q))V(q)h\,dq.$ Taking sup norms and absorbing the first term bounds the left side by $C|h|\int_J\|A_h-A\|dq=o(|h|)$. Thus $D_{x_0}X=V$; dominated convergence in the same integral equation proves continuity of V in $x_0$. The integral FTC [F2] yields $\dot V=A(t)V$ almost everywhere. Repeating on a finite cover by overlapping short intervals gives $C^1$ dependence throughout each common flow domain and continuous dependence in the uniform path norm on trajectories existing through the full interval.

Uniqueness makes the time map from s to t injective. Continuous dependence makes its domain open; solving backward from time t shows its image is open and its inverse is the backward flow, which is $C^1$ by step 3.1. The chain rule [F5] says the derivative of the inverse times V is the identity. Thus the time map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between its open domain and image.

Fix a compact flow tube and a compact set K of states it visits. For a fixed target time t, choose a compact time interval J containing t and the varying start times, with all trajectories in the flow identity remaining in K. For trajectories with the same starting time, the integral equation gives $|X(r;s,y)-X(r;s,z)|\le|y-z|+\int_JL_K(q)|X(q;s,y)-X(q;s,z)|dq$; iterating this inequality yields the spatial Lipschitz bound $|X(t;s,y)-X(t;s,z)|\le e^{\int_JL_K}|y-z|$. For $s,s+h\in J$, the flow identity and the integral equation along the short backward segment give $X(t;s+h,x)=X(t;s,X(s;s+h,x))$ and $|X(s;s+h,x)-x|\le\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K(q)dq$, where the integral is over the unoriented interval. Hence $|X(t;s+h,x)-X(t;s,x)|\le e^{\int_JL_K}\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K(q)dq$. Summing over any disjoint adjacent intervals shows that $s\mapsto X(t;s,x)$ is locally absolutely continuous, uniformly for x in the tube. To identify its derivative, choose a countable dense subset Q of K. By [F6], outside one null set the functions $m_K,L_K$ and $s\mapsto b(s,q)$ for all $q\in Q$ have their values as limits of local averages; also the spatial Lipschitz bound holds at such s. Approximation by q and the common Lipschitz bound show that the averages of $b(r,x)$ over intervals shrinking to s converge to $b(s,x)$ uniformly for $x\in K$. For the solution started at x at time $s+h$, the magnitude bound gives $|X(r;s+h,x)-x|\le\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K=O(|h|)$ uniformly between s and s+h at these Lebesgue points. Replacing $b(r,x)$ by $b(r,X(r;s+h,x))$ in the average contributes at most $|h|^{-1}O(|h|)\int_{[s,s+h]}L_K(r)dr=O(|h|)$. The integral equation therefore gives $[X(s;s+h,x)-x]/h\to-b(s,x)$ uniformly on K. The flow identity $X(t;s+h,x)=X(t;s,X(s;s+h,x))$ and the spatial derivative from step 3.1 yield $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ almost everywhere on the tube. The right side has the integrable local bound $e^{\int_JL_K}m_K(s)$, consistent with and also giving the local absolute continuity.

$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to $v^\varepsilon$ and denote by $D_t$ the open set of initial points whose trajectories exist from time 0 through t, and by $E_t=X_t^\varepsilon(D_t)$ its open image. Fix $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. For $0\le r\le t$ and $x\in D_{r,t}$, the set of states whose trajectories exist from r to t, define $\psi(r,x)=f(X^\varepsilon(t;r,x))$; extend it by zero outside $D_{r,t}$. Since $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compactly contained in $E_t$, its backward images form a compact subset of the flow domain. Thus $\psi$ has compact spatial support uniformly in r, is continuously differentiable in x, and is absolutely continuous in r locally. The start-time derivative from [F2] and the flow identity give $\partial_r\psi=\nabla f(X(t;r,x))\cdot[-D_xX(t;r,x)v_r^\varepsilon(x)]=-v_r^\varepsilon(x)\cdot\nabla_x\psi$ almost everywhere.

For this fixed t define the restricted finite pushforward $
u_t$ on $E_t$ by $
u_t(B)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(\{x\in D_t:X_t^\varepsilon(x)\in B\})$ for Borel $B\subseteq E_t$. The set is Borel because $X_t^\varepsilon$ is continuous on the open domain $D_t$; preimages preserve disjoint unions, so $
u_t$ is a finite Borel measure of mass $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)$. The weak continuity-equation identity extends from smooth compact tests to compactly supported tests that are $C^1$ in x and absolutely continuous in r with locally integrable time derivative: multiply by a time cutoff, convolve in time and space on a fixed compact neighborhood, and pass to the limit. The terms converge because $p^\varepsilon$ is locally bounded, $p^\varepsilon v^\varepsilon$ is locally integrable in time and space by finite action, and the test and its spatial gradient converge uniformly while its time derivative converges in $L^1$. Apply this extension to $\eta(r)\psi(r,x)$ from step 1.1 for every smooth compactly supported time cutoff $\eta$. The transport equation leaves $\int\eta'(r)F(r)dr=0$, so $F(r)=\int\psi(r,x)d\mu_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is constant on $(0,t)$. Continuity of the flow and of $\mu_r^\varepsilon$ extends the identity to r=0,t, giving $\int f(y)d\mu_t^\varepsilon(y)=\int f(X_t^\varepsilon(x))d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)$ for every $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. Uniform mollification extends equality to every $f\in C_c(E_t)$; both measures are finite, so uniform limits pass through their integrals. For a compact $K\subset E_t$, choose n sufficiently large that the closed $1/n$-neighborhood of K is compactly contained in $E_t$ and set $f_n(x)=\max\{0,1-n\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\}$. Then $f_n\in C_c(E_t)$ and $f_n\downarrow\mathbf1_K$, so [F6] gives $
u_t(K)=\mu_t^\varepsilon(K)$. By [F5], both finite Borel measures on the Polish space $E_t$ are inner regular; their agreement on compact sets therefore proves $
u_t=\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$.

For every $r\in(0,T]$, step 2.1 gives equality of the restricted finite measures on $E_r$. Applying it to $y\mapsto\min\{N,|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2\}$ and letting $N\uparrow\infty$ by [F7] yields $\int_{D_r}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)=\int_{E_r}|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)\le\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)$. Let $\mathscr D=\{(r,x):x\in D_r\}$. This domain is relatively open in $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$ and $(r,x)\mapsto X_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is continuous on it: cover any compact trajectory segment through $(r,x)$ by finitely many local flow neighborhoods from [F2] and patch their continuous dependence on the initial point; time continuity follows from the integral equation. Thus the integrand is Borel; extend it by zero off $\mathscr D$. Tonelli [F4] then gives $\int\!\int_0^{\min\{T,\tau(x)\}}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2dr\,d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)\le\int_0^T\!\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)dr<\infty.$ Thus for $\mu_0^\varepsilon$-almost every x the path has finite squared speed integral up to its maximal endpoint. Holder then makes its total path length finite. Such a path is Cauchy at any finite endpoint; it cannot escape every compact set, contradicting [F2] if an endpoint lies in $(0,T)$. At T it has a finite limit and extends continuously to T. Thus $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$.

For each t, step 2.1 identifies $\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$ with $
u_t=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#(\mu_0^\varepsilon|_{D_t})$, where this restricted pushforward is the finite measure defined in step 2.1. Since $D_T\subseteq D_t$ and $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$ by step 3.1, $
u_t(E_t)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)=1$. Hence $\mu_t^\varepsilon(E_t)=1$, and the equality of restricted measures extends to all Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$. Because $D_t$ is open and $X_t^\varepsilon$ is continuous there, extend $X_t^\varepsilon$ to all of $\mathbb R^d$ by setting it to zero off $D_t$; this is Borel and its pushforward is $
u_t$ since $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)=1$. Thus $\mu_t^\varepsilon=(X_t^\varepsilon)_\#\mu_0^\varepsilon$. This proves the claim for every t, with the unique flow given by [F2].
